Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Return correct text unchanged.", "input": "mara: quick question for the clock folks. i picked up a small oak mantel clock at the estate sale on Hawthorn St. last month. the seller said it came from her grandfather's shop, but there isn't a receipt or family note with it. the movement is stamped Ansonia, and the back door has a paper label that says "No. 14, 1907." does that date sound like a model date, or could it just be an inventory number?

theo: Ansonia used a lot of different labels, so i'd treat the paper date as a clue, not a firm date for the whole clock. Is there a date or patent line on the movement plate? Also, photos of the dial, hands and case corners might help narrow down the style. The company made loads of mantel clocks over a long stretch.

mara: i can get photos after work. the face is about 5 inches across, white enamel with black Roman numerals, and the minute hand has a little bend near the tip. case is roughly 11 inches tall. the seller said it ran when she was a kid, which doesn't tell us much, i know.

june: Check the bottom and the inside of the back panel too. Sometimes there’s a paper label tucked under the movement, or a penciled number on the wood. Don't scrape anything off to find it, though. Old paper can be fragile, and the label you found may be useful even if it isn't a date.

luis: On mine the movement plate has the maker name and patent dates, but they weren't the year mine was assembled. If yours has a gong coil, see if there’s a maker mark on that as well. I wouldn't use the gong or movement number by itself to date the case; parts can get changed.

mara: good point about the case and movement not necessarily matching. there's a brass gong at the back, one winding key in the drawer and two little holes on the dial, at 4 and 8. no key marked on the case. the back panel's loose at the top, so i'm trying not to handle it more than i need to.

eLI: For the winding holes, check that the key fits without forcing it. Some old keys are the wrong size, and a key can slip and scratch the dial. If it turns freely, that's one thing; if it catches or feels gritty, stop. A clock that's been sitting may need attention before anyone tries to run it.

theo: Also, don't assume the little bend in the minute hand is damage from use. It may have been bent at some point to clear something, or it could just be a bend. I'd avoid trying to straighten it while it's on the dial. A close photo from straight on would show whether the hands touch.

nina: If you're going to take the movement out, take a few pictures first and keep the screws in a labeled bag. But honestly, if you've never done one, I'd leave it in place for now. The wood case and the enamel dial can be cleaned very differently, and a general cleaner could do more harm than good.

mara: here's what i've noticed so far, in case it's useful: 1) the oak has a dark finish, worn lighter along the right front edge; 2) the glass door has a small chip at the bottom left; 3) the dial has a hairline mark from about 7 toward the center; 4) the pendulum is present, but i haven't tried hanging it.

june: That’s a good list. On the finish, I wouldn't put shellac, oil, or wax on it until you know what’s already there. Even a spot that looks dull can have old varnish on it. For the glass chip, just note where it is so you can tell if it changes; don't push on the edge to test it.

ravi: The label could be an inventory tag from the seller's grandfather's shop, like you said, but there's no way to know from that wording alone. A photo of the back of the movement and the label would be useful. If you post them, include one wider shot too so we can see how the movement sits in the case.

mara: thanks. i don't want to open the movement or clean it yet. i was mostly trying to figure out if 1907 is a reasonable clue, and whether i should look for anything specific before i take it to a repair person. i have a local horologist's name from the historical society, no appointment yet.

theo: I'd write down what came with it, including the key, and mention that you haven't wound it. Ask the horologist to check the movement and the case separately, and whether the hands are rubbing. You can also ask if they recognize the label, but I wouldn't treat their guess as proof of the exact year.

nina: One more thing: keep the clock upright and away from a radiator or sunny window while it's waiting. If you move it, support the case from underneath rather than lifting it by the top ornament. That finial can look sturdier than it is, especially if the glue has aged.

Return correct text unchanged.", "input": "Mara: quick update from the clock room: we finished the first pass through the estate lot this morning. There are 18 clocks on the inventory sheet, including six mantel clocks, four wall clocks, three carriage clocks, and five longcase or bracket clocks. Nothing has been cleaned yet, so the notes reflect what we could see under the dust, not a final condition report.

Jon: The tall oak longcase is marked “J. H. Evans, Bristol” on the dial. Its brass weights and pendulum were wrapped separately in brown paper, and we found the winding key in the bottom drawer. The case has a split near the lower hinge, but the door still closes. I’ve photographed the maker’s mark and the split from both sides.

Leah: I checked the carriage clocks against the boxes. Two have their original leather cases, and one case has a cracked handle. The smallest clock has a silvered dial with Roman numerals and a retailer’s name from Bath; the lettering is partly worn. I haven’t tried winding any of them, since the springs and stops need a closer look first.

Mara: For the record, the blue transferware mantel clock is the one with the loose rear panel, not the clock in the green box. The green-box clock has a porcelain face with a small chip at seven o’clock. We’ve kept both boxes beside their clocks and added matching paper tags, so they won’t get separated during the room move.

Owen: I measured the walnut wall clock at 74 centimeters high, 31 wide, and 14 deep. The painted scene below the dial looks like a harbor, though the bottom edge is faded and I can’t make out the boat details. There’s a label inside the case reading “Regulator No. 42.” The pendulum is present; the key isn’t in the case or the drawer.

Priya: The brass bracket clock has a bell strike and a separate alarm hand. I noted both because the first inventory entry only said “brass clock.” The bell is wrapped in cloth beside the case, and the back door has two old screw holes near the latch. There’s no maker’s name visible on the movement from the angle we checked, so I left that field blank.

Mara: Here’s the room-by-room list for the next inventory pass:
1. East cabinet: six mantel clocks, two boxed parts trays, and the loose winding keys.
2. North wall: four wall clocks, including the walnut clock Owen measured.
3. Worktable: three carriage clocks and their two leather cases.
4. Alcove: five longcase or bracket clocks, with the oak case and brass bracket clock noted separately.
The count is still 18 clocks total. If anyone spots a mismatch, please flag the tag number rather than moving anything.

Jon: I found the tag for the small black mantel clock behind the ledger. It’s AR-116, and the entry says the case is ebonized wood. The finish has a few pale scuffs along the right side, but the feet are all present. There’s a handwritten card with it that reads, “From the front parlor, 1938.” We’ve kept the card in a sleeve with the tag.

Leah: Just adding a detail on the longcase clocks: the painted dial on the pine case has a moon phase disk, while the oak Evans clock has a plain seconds hand. The pine clock’s hood door is off its hinge and resting on a padded shelf. No one has attempted to rehang it. I added the shelf location to the condition notes so it’s easy to find.

Owen: I compared the wall-clock keys with the key ring in the office. One key fits the square arbor on the walnut clock, but I didn’t turn it. Two others are smaller and unmarked, and the remaining key has a tag reading “Workshop.” I’ve put them in a clear envelope marked for the clock room, rather than guessing which clock they belong to.

Mara: Thanks. The estate paperwork lists the clocks as coming from the house on Mill Lane, but it doesn’t give dates or purchase prices. A folder labeled “Repairs” contains two receipts from a shop in York, dated 1986 and 1991; both mention a mantel clock, but neither receipt has a model number. I’ve noted the folder reference without matching either receipt to a specific clock.

Priya: The glass on the square dial clock is convex and has a cloudy patch near the lower edge. The minute hand looks slightly bent in the photo, though it may just be the viewing angle. I took another picture straight on and left the first image in the folder too. The small brass finial was on the same shelf, but there’s no tag linking it to that clock yet.

Jon: The paper tags are holding up well, but the string on AR-109 is slipping against the case handle. I replaced the string and copied the number onto a fresh tag, then kept the old tag in the envelope with the notes. AR-109 is the mahogany mantel clock with the cream dial and black Arabic numerals. Its glass door opens from the left.

Leah: I’ve put the photo filenames into the shared sheet, including the close-ups of the worn Bath retailer’s name and the Bristol maker’s mark. The overview images show each clock beside its tag, and the detail images cover visible chips, splits, missing keys, or detached parts. There are no movement photographs yet. That can wait until the clocks are examined at the workbench.

Mara: That’s all for today. The room is locked, the two loose doors are on padded shelves, and the paperwork is back in the labeled folder. Tomorrow’s list is to verify the tags against the sheet, check the count once more, and record any parts we find in the drawers.
